### P-0102 v1 — Korea AI Basic Act: the Enforcement Decree adds capability and risk criteria to the 10²⁶ FLOPs threshold

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `c79e8d76e97c`

**Change**

- **`kr-ai` · coverage · thresh**

  Current:

  > Defines high-performance AI as cumulative compute ≥10²⁶ FLOPs (matching California SB 53 and NY RAISE, higher than the EU AI Act's 10²⁵). High-impact AI is defined separately by use-case rather than compute.

  Proposed:

  > The Act's safety duties (Art. 32) cover systems above a compute threshold set by decree. The Enforcement Decree (Art. 24, in force Jan 22, 2026) requires cumulative compute ≥10²⁶ FLOPs (matching California SB 53 and NY RAISE, higher than the EU AI Act's 10²⁵) plus state-of-the-art technology and risks with broad, serious effects on life, safety and fundamental rights. High-impact AI is defined separately by use-case rather than compute.

- **`kr-ai` · context**

  Current:

  > Korea's first horizontal AI law: tiered obligations on high-impact AI and high-performance AI (≥10²⁶ FLOPs), risk management plans, lifecycle reporting to MSIT, mandatory generative-AI labelling, and a state AI Safety Research Institute. Penalty caps are deliberately low — the Act emphasises guidance over deterrence, mirroring Japan's approach and contrasting with the EU's prescriptive route.

  Proposed:

  > Korea's first horizontal AI law: tiered obligations on high-impact AI and high-performance AI (≥10²⁶ FLOPs plus capability and risk criteria), risk management plans, lifecycle reporting to MSIT, mandatory generative-AI labelling, and a state AI Safety Research Institute. Penalty caps are deliberately low — the Act emphasises guidance over deterrence, mirroring Japan's approach and contrasting with the EU's prescriptive route.

**Why it matters:** Compute alone does not trigger the duties. The decree's three criteria are cumulative, so fewer models are covered than a pure 10²⁶ test would suggest.

**Reasoning:** Act Art. 32(1) delegates the compute standard to Presidential Decree. Decree Art. 24(1) requires all of: ≥10^26 FLOPs, most-advanced technology, and broad, serious risk. Decree Addenda Art. 1 sets entry into force on 22 Jan 2026.

**Evidence**

### P-0103 v1 — Korea AI Basic Act · Accountability: oversight sits with MSIT; the AI Safety Research Institute supports rather than oversees

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `d9b58cda6cc1`

**Change**

- **`kr-ai` · coverage · acct**

  Current:

  > Notification duties to MSIT, oversight by the new AI Safety Research Institute, and user complaint mechanisms. Enforcement teeth deliberately weak — penalty caps ~$21k per violation.

  Proposed:

  > Safety-duty results go to MSIT, which can investigate (including on reports or complaints) and order violations stopped or corrected (Art. 40); the AI Safety Research Institute supports safety work rather than overseeing it. Enforcement teeth deliberately weak — fines capped at ₩30M (~$21k) (Art. 43).

**Why it matters:** The note credits the AI Safety Research Institute with oversight. Under the Act the Institute is a research and support body that MSIT 'may operate'. Investigation and corrective orders belong to MSIT.

**Reasoning:** Art. 12 lists the Institute's tasks: research, standards, international cooperation and support for Art. 32 safety. Art. 32(2) requires results to be submitted to MSIT. Art. 40 gives MSIT investigation (triggered by findings, reports or complaints) and stop or correct orders. Art. 43 caps fines at KRW 30M.

### P-0104 v1 — Japan AI Promotion Act: link the Cabinet Office page instead of a law-firm alert

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `d1f463114414`

**Change**

- **`jp-ai` · link**

  Current:

  > https://www.whitecase.com/insight-alert/japans-first-ai-legislation-becomes-law-focus-promoting-research-and-development-no

  Proposed:

  > https://www8.cao.go.jp/cstp/ai/ai_act/ai_act.html

**Why it matters:** The current link is a White & Case client alert. The government page links the official text on e-Gov and gives the promulgation and entry-into-force dates.

  > Sectoral guidance issued by the AI Strategic Headquarters under the Cabinet Office, with each sector regulator translating high-level principles into industry-specific expectations. No horizontal deployment rules.

  Proposed:

### P-0106 v1 — New entry: US FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925), a bipartisan federal frontier-AI bill with state preemption

`addition` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `6daabe7d9e6e`

**Change**

- **New entry `us-frontier-act`** — US FRONTIER Act · Layer 2 · jur `us` · pow 2 · proposed · https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr9925ih/html/BILLS-119hr9925ih.htm

> H.R. 9925, bipartisan House bill introduced Jul 23, 2026 (Obernolte, Trahan). Frontier models >10²⁶ FLOPs: published frameworks, annual third-party audits, 72-hour incident reports, licensed verifiers for the largest developers; up to $1M per violation. Would preempt state frontier-transparency, audit and incident-reporting rules.

> Would create a federal frontier-AI regime under a new Commerce Under Secretary for AI Security. Large frontier developers would have to publish, follow and annually audit a frontier AI framework and publish a transparency report at each deployment. Very large ones would also retain a licensed independent verification organization. The Commerce Secretary could order a halt to development or deployment that presents an imminent catastrophic risk. The preemption clause covers the ground of state laws such as SB 53 and RAISE (frontier risk transparency, third-party auditing, incident reporting) but leaves deployment, child-safety and state-procurement rules to the states. It is a congressional route to the national standard EO 14365 calls for, with binding duties the EO does not create.

  - _thresh_: Frontier models trained with >10²⁶ FLOPs. Obligations scale with developer size: large (>$50M revenue and ≥$1B AI development spending over 36 months) and very large (>$5B and ≥$10B).
  - _eval_: Annual independent compliance audits for large frontier developers. Very large developers retain a licensed independent verification organization for ongoing assessment of their framework, risk monitoring and mitigations, including internal use.
  - _timing_: Transparency report before or at deployment of each new or substantially modified frontier model. Critical safety incidents reported within 72 hours (24 hours to law enforcement for imminent risk to life).
  - _mit_: Frontier AI frameworks must set risk thresholds, assess each model against them and decide on deployment and internal use; minimum framework requirements are set by regulation.
  - _sec_: Frameworks must cover cybersecurity for non-public model weights; weight exfiltration is a reportable critical safety incident.
  - _halt_: The Commerce Secretary may issue emergency orders suspending or restricting development, deployment or internal use of a frontier model that presents an imminent catastrophic risk.
  - _acct_: Audit reports go to the Under Secretary, the Attorney General and opted-in state attorneys general. Civil penalties up to $1M per violation, enforced by the Attorney General and opted-in state AGs.
  - _update_: Frameworks reviewed at least annually, with a justification published within 30 days of any material change; framework regulations reviewed yearly.

- **new connection `us-frontier-act` ↔ `ca-sb53`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > Would preempt state frontier-transparency, audit and incident-reporting duties such as SB 53's

- **new connection `us-frontier-act` ↔ `ny-raise`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > Would preempt state frontier-transparency, audit and incident-reporting duties such as RAISE's

- **new connection `us-frontier-act` ↔ `us-preempt`**

  Current:

  > _(absent)_

  Proposed:

  > Legislative route to the preemptive national standard EO 14365 calls for

**Why it matters:** This is the first bipartisan federal bill to impose frontier-specific safety duties: frameworks, audits, incident reporting, licensed verifiers and emergency halt orders. It would also preempt the state laws the map tracks (SB 53, RAISE). As a formally introduced bill it qualifies as 'proposed' under RUBRIC §1. It was introduced after the map's June snapshot.

**Reasoning:** Every element is taken from the introduced text on govinfo: sponsors and date, definitions (§2), framework, audit, transparency and incident duties (§4), licensed verifiers (§5), emergency orders (§8) and preemption (§9).

### P-0107 v1 — METR's nine elements are not the map's nine categories: say the categories are adapted

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `163b36ea9a1c`

**Change**

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > is a taxonomy of nine elements that frontier AI safety frameworks address: capability thresholds, model evaluations, capability elicitation, timing and frequency, weight security, deployment mitigations, conditions for halting, accountability, and updating policies. This map applies the taxonomy as an orthogonal filter

  Proposed:

  > identifies nine elements that frontier AI safety policies share: capability thresholds, model weight security, deployment mitigations, conditions for halting deployment, conditions for halting development, full capability elicitation during evaluations, timing and frequency of evaluations, accountability, and updating policies over time. This map adapts them into nine coverage categories — merging the two halting conditions and adding model evaluations as a category of its own — and applies them as an orthogonal filter

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > The orthogonal coverage analysis applies METR's nine elements (originally a taxonomy of corporate safety frameworks) to the full set of mechanisms.

  Proposed:

  > The orthogonal coverage analysis applies nine categories adapted from METR's common elements (originally a taxonomy of corporate safety frameworks) to the full set of mechanisms.

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > applied across METR's nine common elements of frontier AI safety policies.</p>

  Proposed:

  > applied across nine categories adapted from METR's common elements of frontier AI safety policies.</p>

**Why it matters:** The FAQ tells readers (and LLMs that ingest the JSON-LD) that METR's taxonomy consists of the map's nine categories. METR's own list differs: it has two halting elements and no separate 'model evaluations' element. Citing METR for a list it does not contain misattributes the map's own design choice.

**Reasoning:** METR's Dec 2025 page lists its nine components verbatim (metr-ce#thresh … #update): halting appears twice (deployment, development) and evaluations are discussed inside the other elements (metr-ce#eval) rather than listed. The map's categories therefore adapt METR's list. The edits keep the existing wording and add 'adapted'.

### P-0109 v1 — Thresholds gap: no current lab framework tracks autonomous replication; revenue floors apply only to the US state laws

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `1588fd0a78f9`

**Linked:** P-0037, P-0038, P-0039, P-0041, P-0057, P-0102

**Change**

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > The labs set capability thresholds (CBRN, cyber, autonomous replication, AI R&D); the binding regulations set eligibility thresholds (10²⁵ or 10²⁶ FLOPs plus revenue floors).

  Proposed:

  > The labs set capability thresholds (CBRN, cyber, AI R&D, loss of control); the binding regulations set eligibility thresholds (10²⁵ or 10²⁶ FLOPs, plus a $500M revenue floor for the main US state duties).

**Why it matters:** The example list describes the lab frameworks of 2023–24. OpenAI moved autonomous replication to an untracked research category in v2, and the current Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta and xAI frameworks do not use it, while loss of control/misalignment now appears in most. 'Plus revenue floors' implies the EU AI Act has one; it does not.

**Reasoning:** Current domains: Anthropic RSP v3.4 rows (S-0006#5: chem/bio, misaligned AI in high-stakes settings, automated R&D); OpenAI v2 tracks bio/chem, cyber, AI self-improvement and lists Autonomous Replication and Adaptation among Research Categories (S-0095#2, S-0095#4); GDM v3.1 CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, ML R&D and misalignment (S-0102#3, S-0102#7); Meta v2 chem/bio, cyber, loss of control (S-0107#2); xAI CBRN, cyber, loss of control, harmful manipulation (S-0108#2). EU presumption is compute only (S-0002#10); the $500M floor is in SB 53 (S-0150#4) and RAISE (S-0033#9) for large frontier developers, while SB 53's 10²⁶ tier alone triggers transparency and incident duties (P-0057).

### P-0110 v1 — Evaluations gap: the AI Act requires evaluation with adversarial testing, not third-party evaluation; the GPAI Code adds external evaluation

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `9448ef802fa7`

**Linked:** P-0031

**Change**

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > The EU AI Act requires it for systemic-risk GPAI.

  Proposed:

  > The EU AI Act requires model evaluations with adversarial testing for systemic-risk GPAI, but external testing only as appropriate; the GPAI Code goes further and calls for independent external evaluation.

**Why it matters:** 'It' refers to mandatory third-party evaluation; Article 55 does not mandate third-party evaluation, so the sentence overstates the one binding example the gap gives.

**Reasoning:** Art. 55(1)(a) requires model evaluation including adversarial testing (S-0002#14); recital 114 says this happens 'as appropriate, through internal or independent external testing' (eu-aia#rec114); Annex XI asks systemic-risk providers to describe 'internal and/or external' adversarial testing. The GPAI Code (non-binding) requires independent external evaluations unless exceptions apply (S-0044#8).

**Evidence**

- **S-0002** Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Official Journal — <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-06 · access: ok via browser · adopted 2024-06-13, published 2024-07-12, in_force 2024-08-01
  Art. 55(1)(a):
  > perform model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing of the model with a view to identifying and mitigating systemic risks;
  _Supports:_ Art. 55(1)(a) evaluation duty
- **S-0002** Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Official Journal — <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-06 · access: ok via browser · adopted 2024-06-13, published 2024-07-12, in_force 2024-08-01
  Recital 114:
  > including conducting and documenting adversarial testing of models, also, as appropriate, through internal or independent external testing.
  _Supports:_ external testing only as appropriate
- **S-0002** Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Official Journal — <https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-06 · access: ok via browser · adopted 2024-06-13, published 2024-07-12, in_force 2024-08-01
  Annex XI, Section 2, point 2:
  > Where applicable, a detailed description of the measures put in place for the purpose of conducting internal and/or external adversarial testing (e.g. red teaming), model adaptations, including alignment and fine-tuning.
  _Supports:_ internal and/or external adversarial testing
- **S-0044** GPAI Code of Practice: Safety and Security chapter (Jul 2025) — <https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redirection/document/118119>
  primary · retrieved 2026-11-06 · access: ok · published 2025-07-10
  Appendix 3.5 Independent external model evaluations:
  > In addition to internal model evaluations, Signatories will ensure that adequately qualified independent external evaluators conduct model evaluations pursuant to this Appendix 3, with regards to the systemic risk, unless: (1) the model is a similarly safe or safer model pursuant to Appendix 2.2; or (2) Signatories fail to appoint adequately qualified independent external evaluators
  _Supports:_ GPAI Code external evaluation

**Carried over unchanged, not re-verified:** Korea's Framework Act requires risk management plans; Everywhere else, evaluations happen because labs publish them, AISIs request them under voluntary access agreements, or independent evaluators (METR, Apollo) do them.

**Uncertainty:** The AI Office could expect external testing in practice through the Code; the Act's text does not require it.

### P-0111 v1 — Elicitation gap: the GPAI Code requires elicitation explicitly, and it is not a statute

### P-0112 v1 — Timing gap: Illinois adds 72-hour incident reporting from 2027; the EU duty is GPAI serious-incident reporting, not AI Office post-market monitoring

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `2aaeeca36448`

**Linked:** P-0055, P-0066, P-0095, P-0099

**Applied together with:** P-0066

**Change**

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > California SB 53 (15 days), NY RAISE (72 hours), Korea (lifecycle reporting), and the EU AI Office\'s post-market monitoring are the binding instances. Outside those four, no statutory incident reporting for frontier models exists.

  Proposed:

  > California SB 53 (15 days), NY RAISE and Illinois (72 hours, from 2027), Korea (lifecycle reporting), and the EU AI Act\'s serious-incident reporting for systemic-risk GPAI are the binding instances. Outside these, no statutory incident reporting for frontier models exists.

### P-0113 v1 — Weight-security gap: SB 53 (and RAISE, Illinois) require frameworks to cover securing unreleased model weights

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `982394064686`

**Linked:** P-0023, P-0075

**Applied together with:** P-0066

**Change**

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > BIS export controls touch the adjacent question of who can access frontier-capable hardware. No US state, no UK statute, and no other binding instrument covers weight security directly.

  Proposed:

  > California SB 53 requires the published frameworks of large frontier developers to describe how they secure unreleased model weights, and NY RAISE (2027) and Illinois (2028) copy that duty, but none sets a security level. BIS export controls touch the adjacent question of who can access frontier-capable hardware. No UK statute and no other binding instrument covers weight security directly.

**Why it matters:** The text says no US state covers weight security. SB 53, in force since Jan 2026, makes 'cybersecurity practices to secure unreleased model weights' a required part of each large frontier developer's framework, which the developer must comply with; RAISE and Illinois use the same wording.

**Reasoning:** SB 53 §22757.12(a)(7) (sb53#a7) within the framework duty to write, implement and comply (S-0150#5); RAISE §1421(1)(g) (raise#g; effective 1 Jan 2027, S-0033#3); Illinois §10(a)(7) (il#a7; framework duty from 1 Jan 2028, S-0170#5). None prescribes a security level.

### P-0114 v1 — Halting gap: China can order services suspended; lab halting commitments have weakened (Anthropic, Meta)

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: medium · change-hash `5a144464f807`

**Linked:** P-0022, P-0037, P-0038, P-0039, P-0041, P-0097

**Change**

- **`index.html`**

  Current:

  > The EU AI Office can order recall (Aug 2026 onwards). The GPAI Code calls for halting at systemic-risk thresholds. Seoul commitments asked labs to commit to it. Every lab framework includes it. That\'s essentially the whole list. No US state, no other national statute, no other multilateral instrument can compel a frontier developer to pause.

  Proposed:

  > The EU AI Office can order recall (Aug 2026 onwards). China\'s GenAI Measures let regulators order a non-compliant service suspended. The GPAI Code calls for halting at systemic-risk thresholds. Seoul commitments asked labs to commit to it. Every lab framework includes halting conditions, though several have weakened: Anthropic ties its delay commitments to what competitors do, and Meta\'s v2 replaced "stop" with "develop with mitigations". That\'s essentially the whole list. No US state, and no other frontier-specific statute or multilateral instrument, can compel a frontier developer to pause.

**Why it matters:** The map's own China entry says firms have had services suspended, and Art. 21 of the GenAI Measures provides for ordering suspension — a compelled pause the gap says does not exist. 'Every lab framework includes it' no longer conveys that Anthropic's RSP v3 made delays competitor-dependent and Meta's v2 dropped 'stop'.

**Reasoning:** S-0290#6 (Art. 21: ordered to suspend the relevant services); EU recall power S-0002#20, enforcement from 2 Aug 2026 S-0280#1; GPAI Code Measure 4.2 (S-0044#3); Seoul commitment IV (S-0034#8); RSP v3.4 Appendix A (S-0006#12); Meta v2 change log (S-0107#5); OpenAI v2 Critical halt (S-0095#6).

### P-0116 v1 — Default gap text: Illinois enacted mandatory third-party audits (2028) and incident reporting; the EU AI Act already requires GPAI incident reporting

`change` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **accepted** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: high · change-hash `fd07cdbf6d23`

**Linked:** P-0066

**Applied together with:** P-0066

**Change**

- **`index.html` (2 occurrences)**

  Current:

  > Mandatory third-party auditing, compute KYC, statutory incident reporting beyond California and (from 2027) New York, liability rules for harmful outputs, and international verification regimes are proposed somewhere — binding nowhere yet.

  Proposed:

  > Compute KYC, liability rules for harmful outputs, and international verification regimes are proposed somewhere — binding nowhere yet. Mandatory third-party auditing of frontier developers is enacted only in Illinois (from 2028), and statutory incident reporting for frontier models only in the EU, California, and (from 2027) New York and Illinois.

**Why it matters:** This is the panel's default text. Two of its 'binding nowhere' items are now binding law: Illinois requires large frontier developers to retain a third party for an annual independent compliance audit (from 2028) and to report critical incidents within 72 hours (from 2027); and the EU AI Act has required serious-incident reporting from systemic-risk GPAI providers since Aug 2025, which the map's own gap:acct names.

**Reasoning:** Illinois Act §25(a) penalises failure to have a third party perform an independent audit under §10(d) (il#audit, S-0170#8), §15(c) 72-hour reports (S-0170#9), effective 1 Jan 2027 (S-0170#13); AI Act Art. 55(1)(c) (S-0002#15). No audit duty in SB 53 or RAISE (S-0150#17, S-0033#18).

**Evidence**

### P-0108 v1 — Category definitions for thresholds, timing, mitigations (and evaluations) depart from METR's meaning

`question` · evidence: **Verified against inspected external sources** · decision: **withdrawn** (v1, 2026-10-10) · confidence: medium · change-hash `4f53cda18c2b`

**Question for you:** METR defines capability thresholds as 'Thresholds at which specific AI capabilities would pose severe risk and require new mitigations'; the map says 'Levels at which obligations or risks trigger', which also takes in regulatory eligibility thresholds (compute, revenue). METR's timing element is 'when and how often evaluations must be performed'; the map says 'When evaluations and obligations apply'. METR's deployment mitigations are 'access and model-level measures applied to prevent the unauthorized use of a model's dangerous capabilities'; the map says 'Refusals, monitoring, content controls'. 'Model evaluations' is not one of METR's nine. Options: (a) keep the map's broader definitions and say they are adapted (pairs with metr-taxonomy; recommended); (b) restore METR's meaning, e.g. thresh 'Capability levels that pose severe risk and require new mitigations', timing 'When and how often evaluations are performed', mit 'Access and model-level measures that prevent misuse of dangerous capabilities' — then coverage notes that rely on the broader meaning (e.g. compute-eligibility thresholds under thresh, obligation timing under timing, content moderation under mit) become stretches to mark; (c) METR wording plus a short adaptation note, e.g. thresh 'Capability levels that pose severe risk and require new mitigations (here also regulatory compute thresholds)'.

**Why it matters:** The category definitions are the page's description of what each filter means; where they diverge from METR while citing METR, readers may take the map's broader categories for METR's.

**Reasoning:** Compared each map definition with METR's component definition (metr-ce). Elicitation, weight security, halting, accountability (METR includes transparency, metr-ce#acct2) and updating match in meaning; thresholds, timing and mitigations are broadened; evaluations is the map's own addition.

**Evidence**

- **S-0204** Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies — <https://metr.org/common-elements>

  Introduction, components list:

  _Supports:_ METR's threshold definition is capability-based

  Link resolves to the Panel site. Res. 79/325 adopted 26 Aug 2025 sets up a 40-member Panel and an annual Dialogue. Co-chairs are Bengio and Ressa.
